You are an independent benchmark designer. You have NOT seen the skill implementation you are benchmarking — only its outcome contract, in `contract.md`. Do not guess or reconstruct implementation details; test outcomes.

Design a benchmark of exactly 8 tasks for a Claude Code agent, testing the full contract: ordinary use, difficult situations, edge cases, realistic variations, and the activation boundary (include at least 1 task where the capability must correctly stay silent / not fire). Tasks must be executable by a headless coding agent inside an empty sandbox git repo with standard file tools and NO network, NO live services, NO MCP servers, NO running dev processes. When a task needs an environment (config files, a small repo, logs, a transcript), specify every fixture file inline. The contestant also runs NON-INTERACTIVELY: no human can answer questions mid-run, so a task may test how well the agent elicits or proceeds without answers, but must not require live human replies to be completable.

Write `benchmark.json` in your working directory:
{
  "tasks": [
    {
      "id": "T1",
      "kind": "ordinary|hard|edge|variation|activation-negative",
      "prompt": "<exact text the contestant agent receives — realistic user phrasing, no mention of skills, benchmarks, or evaluation>",
      "fixtures": {"relative/path.ext": "<full file content>", ...},
      "packet": {
        "situation": "<what the user asked, restated for a judge>",
        "contract_extract": "<the parts of the contract that bear on this task>",
        "invariants": ["<objective facts a correct result must satisfy>"],
        "priorities": "<which qualities dominate when results differ>",
        "disqualifiers": ["<failures that void an answer>"]
      }
    }, ...
  ]
}

Rules:
- Realistic: prompts a real user in a real repo would plausibly type.
- Solvable: a strong agent with the right knowledge can succeed inside the sandbox; nothing requires live infrastructure.
- No leakage: packets describe success, never a gold answer to copy, and never wording that fingerprints any particular implementation.
- Where multiple good answers exist, the packet defines success criteria, not one blessed output.
- Fixtures must be complete and internally consistent.
Write ONLY benchmark.json (valid JSON, no markdown fences).

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

1	# Outcome Contract
2	
3	## 1. Purpose
4	
5	Give a software project a durable, on-disk record of its own intent and progress, and make an
6	assistant work from that record instead of from conversation memory. The skill establishes a set of
7	persistent project documents — what is being built and for whom, how the product should sound and
8	look, what technology it uses, what coding standards apply, and what development conventions govern
9	the work — decomposes upcoming work into individually specified and planned units, executes those
10	plans while keeping the recorded progress synchronized with reality, reports that progress on
11	demand, and can undo work at any granularity. The value is continuity and auditability across
12	sessions and people: anyone can open the project cold and see what was decided, what is done, what
13	is underway, and what is next.
14	
15	## 2. Success
16	
17	Observable from outside the assistant:
18	
19	- A single predictable location in the project holds the context documents, an index of work units,
20	  and, for each unit, its specification, its plan, and its recorded status. Both a person and a
21	  program can read that state.
22	- The context documents cover product intent, the product's voice and visual character, the
23	  technology in use, per-language coding standards, and development conventions.
24	- The recorded conventions settle at least: the verification threshold work must meet, the
25	  granularity at which work is committed, and where per-item work summaries are kept.
26	- A unit's specification states how completion will be verified, and that is what execution checks
27	  against before recording anything as done.
28	- Every plan item, at every level of grouping, carries a status marker, and those markers match what
29	  has actually been built and verified. Markers distinguish at least: not started, underway, done.
30	- The index, the per-unit status, and the plan agree with one another at all times; a reader
31	  consulting any one of them draws the same conclusion.
32	- A progress query returns an accurate roll-up — how much is done, what is being worked on, what
33	  comes next, what is obstructed — purely by reading the record, not from chat history. Obstructions
34	  met during execution are written into that record, not merely mentioned aloud.
35	- Each meaningful state change is captured in the project's revision history, so that history
36	  explains both the code and the decisions.
37	- Any recorded unit — or a group or single item within one — can later be undone, with the code and
38	  the recorded status returning to a consistent prior state, without discarding history.
39	- Content the assistant drafts on the user's behalf — project documents, a unit's specification, its
40	  plan, its title — is presented for approval and revised before it is written.
41	- Initialization leaves behind a project that is documented *and* has one work unit already
42	  specified and planned; a run interrupted partway resumes where it stopped rather than restarting.
43	- On completing a unit, the user is offered its disposition: retain the artifacts but drop it from
44	  the active index, remove it entirely, or leave it in place.
45	- After any operation, the user is told what state things are in and what the available next moves
46	  are.
47	
48	## 3. Qualities ranked
49	
50	1. **Truthfulness of recorded state.** The record is the product. A plan that claims work is
51	   finished when it is not is worse than no record, because downstream operations, reports, and undo
52	   all trust it.
53	2. **User authority over content and destructive acts.** Everything the assistant authors on the
54	   user's behalf must reflect the user's intent, not the assistant's invention, and be seen before
55	   it lands; irreversible or wide-reaching actions must be previewed and consented to. This
56	   constrains *how* the work is done: the owner wants the human deciding, the assistant drafting.
57	3. **Recoverability.** Nothing done should be a one-way door. History is preserved rather than
58	   rewritten so that an undo is itself auditable and itself reversible.
59	4. **Structural stability.** The layout, naming scheme, and status vocabulary are the interface
60	   between separate operations and between sessions. They must be stable and discoverable, not
61	   clever.
62	
63	## 4. Hard constraints
64	
65	- All persistent artifacts live in one dedicated location within the project, readable directly by a
66	  person, with the structured status data readable by a program.
67	- Each work unit is addressed by a stable, human-meaningful name that is unique across the project;
68	  collisions are detected before creation.
69	- Every generated plan item, including nested ones, is created with a status marker already present.
70	  Plans carry an intermediate grouping level between the unit and the individual item — verification
71	  checkpoints and undo both operate at that level.
72	- Elicitation is bounded and easy to escape: a small number of focused questions, asked one at a
73	  time, each offering a few concrete options alongside a free-form answer. Where the questions
74	  define the project as a whole, the user may also hand the remaining answers to the assistant.
75	- Choices about development conventions are put to the user with the owner's recommended default
76	  named, not as bare either/ors.
77	- Initialization detects whether the project is new or pre-existing and adapts: for a pre-existing
78	  one, detected facts are stated back for confirmation rather than elicited from scratch; a new
79	  project is placed under revision control as part of setup.
80	- Initialization records a durable checkpoint after each step and resumes from the last one recorded.
81	- Inspection of a pre-existing codebase happens only with permission, is read-only, honors the
82	  project's own exclusion rules, and is summarized back before anything is generated from it.
83	- Any operation that depends on the project context must first confirm that context exists; if it
84	  does not, it does not proceed and names the initializing operation instead of improvising.
85	- The unit to execute is never chosen unilaterally: a named target is confirmed with the user
86	  first; absent one, the incomplete units are presented and the assistant waits for an explicit
87	  choice.
88	- The target to undo is chosen the same way: a named target is confirmed; absent one, candidates are
89	  presented — preferring work currently underway, and always allowing the user to name something
90	  else instead.
91	- Recorded conventions govern planning as well as execution: if they call for tests to precede
92	  implementation, the generated plan reflects that, and so does the run.
93	- Execution proceeds continuously through a unit's plan, pausing only where the recorded conventions
94	  define a verification checkpoint at a group boundary, or on error.
95	- Undo previews the exact set of changes it will reverse and requires confirmation before acting; it
96	  preserves history rather than rewriting it; it must still find the recorded work when the
97	  underlying history has been rewritten or its identifiers no longer match. When it cannot complete
98	  cleanly it stops, tells the user precisely how to finish or abandon the operation by hand, and
99	  waits. A declined or abandoned undo leaves the working state untouched, and abandoning it remains
100	  available throughout.
101	- On failure during execution, the run stops, reports plainly, and offers the user a choice of how to
102	  continue.
103	
104	## 5. Must never
105	
106	- Record an item as complete when it failed, was skipped, or was not verified.
107	- Leave the index, the per-unit status, and the plan disagreeing about the same unit of work.
108	- Write a drafted specification, plan, or project document without first showing it to the user.
109	- Delete a user's work without explicit confirmation; permanent deletion requires confirmation
110	  escalated beyond a single yes.
111	- Rewrite or discard existing revision history in order to undo something.
112	- Read or analyze an existing codebase before being granted permission.
113	- Change the project-level context documents silently; each proposed change is shown and approved
114	  individually.
115	- Overwrite or re-run initialization over a project that is already initialized.
116	- Continue past a missing prerequisite, an unresolved conflict, or a failed step by guessing.
117	- Fabricate project intent, requirements, or acceptance criteria and present them as the user's.
118	
119	## 6. Activation boundary
120	
121	Triggers only on explicit, by-name invocation of one of its operations. It is a command family, not
122	an ambient behavior.
123	
124	Within the family: the initializing operation is the only one valid on an unestablished project and
125	is invalid on an established one. All others require the established context and must decline,
126	pointing at initialization, when it is absent. Execution additionally requires at least one
127	incomplete unit of work; undo requires at least one recorded unit.
128	
129	## 7. Derived
130	
131	Not stated by the owner; inferred from the shape of the operations.
132	
133	- Reporting progress is read-only — the reporting operation has no step that changes anything.
134	- Because the operations are defined only as named commands, nothing about this system — its
135	  existence, its layout, or its vocabulary — should surface during ordinary development work unless
136	  the user names an operation.
